title: Self-Adaptive Quantum State Topology Optimization
abstract: Quantum state topology optimization is a challenging task requiring precise control over quantum states. This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive quantum state topology optimization algorithm, leveraging the inherent properties of quantum states to guide the optimization process. We propose a framework that dynamically adjusts the quantum state parameters based on feedback from the optimization process, enabling a more efficient and robust optimization. The core mechanism centers around a quantum state evolution driven by a feedback loop, resulting in improved performance compared to existing classical optimization techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations and provide a detailed analysis of its performance characteristics. The algorithm's adaptability and efficiency make it a promising approach for tackling complex quantum optimization problems.

title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithm Design for Large-Scale Data Compression
abstract: Traditional data compression algorithms, primarily based on classical statistical modeling, often struggle to achieve optimal compression ratios when dealing with large-scale, complex datasets. This paper proposes a novel approach to data compression—quantum-inspired algorithm design—that addresses this limitation. The core idea is to simulate the principles of quantum superposition, allowing the compression system to simultaneously evaluate and consider multiple compression strategies based on the probabilistic characteristics of the data. title: Quantum-Inspired Constraint Programming for Compiler Optimization
abstract: Quantum-Inspired Constraint Programming (QICP) presents a novel paradigm for compiler optimization, inspired by quantum mechanics, aiming to achieve performance gains through reduced computational complexity. This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum phenomena – specifically, superposition, entanglement, and interference – to represent and optimize constraint-based programming languages. We detail the core mechanism of translating the constraint-based language into a quantum-inspired representation, focusing on identifying optimal program structures and minimizing the number of computations. The paper analyzes the theoretical implications and initial experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of QICP in optimizing key aspects of code execution. This research highlights a potential paradigm shift in software development, moving beyond traditional algorithmic approaches towards a fundamentally different way of thinking about program design and optimization.

title: Modeling What Changes: Sparse, Residual World Models for Object-Centric Manipulation
abstract: Monolithic world models predict the entire next state at every step, spending capacity re-predicting the static majority of a scene and injecting error into it. We ask whether explicitly modeling change (a per-object change gate plus a residual delta head that perturbs only the objects the gate flags) is a more effective and interpretable bias for physical prediction and control. On a MuJoCo tabletop pushing benchmark scaling from 3 to 8 objects, the sparse/residual model predicts next-state poses 2.5 to 4.6 times more accurately than a dense multilayer perceptron at 8.6 to 11.1 times fewer parameters, sustains change-detection F1 of 0.80 to 0.87 where the dense baseline is degenerate, transfers across object counts with zero retraining (99.4 percent F1 retention), and reaches about 90 percent of its full-data accuracy with a quarter of the data. In autoregressive rollout it compounds far less error, hugging the no-motion floor while the dense model drifts. Finally, inside a sampling-based planner, prediction-only models fail (though a true-simulator oracle solves the task with the identical planner, confirming the planner is sound), but once featurized and trained for the states a planner visits, the sparse model begins to plan (0.23 plus or minus 0.06 success over three seeds) while the dense monolith stays at zero at every seed. Modeling what changes, rather than re-predicting the whole world, is a simple, effective bias for object-centric physical AI; code, data generators, and all checkpoints will be released upon publication.

title: On commensurations of pro-C groups
abstract: We study commensurations of pro-C groups, where C is an extension-closed variety of finite groups. We also consider obtain a structural result on virtual retracts of pro-C groups.

title: OntoExtend: A Framework for Requirement-Driven and Scalable Ontology Extension with LLMs
abstract: Ontology extension refers to the process of enriching an existing ontology in response to emerging requirements, making it more complete. This task is a resource-intensive and error-prone process. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising performance on generating ontologies from scratch, but current approaches rarely tie ontology extension explicitly to requirements or reusable core models, and offer limited, systematic evaluation of LLM outputs. This paper introduces OntoExtend, a requirements-driven framework for ontology extension with LLMs. It uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over relevant input ontologies and requirements in the form of competency questions to propose grounded extensions. We evaluate OntoExtend on 39 CQs from two use cases: a public EU-project ontology, Onto-DESIDE, and an industrial ontology from Bosch. The generated fragments show few structural issues, satisfy all functional evaluation tests, and are rated by ontology engineers as requiring minor to moderate revision before integration. These results suggest that OntoExtend is useful as a drafting assistant for requirement-driven ontology extension in real world scenarios, while remaining sensitive to CQ specificity and modelling profile.

title: An Explainable Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Enhanced Early Detection and Comprehensive Staging of Breast Cancer
abstract: Breast cancer remains a major global health challenge, requiring accurate and interpretable diagnostic systems for reliable clinical deployment. This paper proposes an Explainable Hybrid Machine Learning (XML) framework that integrates advanced feature extraction with interpretable classification techniques for early breast cancer detection and staging. Using benchmark datasets including WDBC, BreakHis, and CBIS-DDSM, the framework applies CLAHE-based preprocessing, PCA, and SHAP-driven Recursive Feature Elimination (SHAP-RFE) to generate an optimized Hybrid Feature Vector (HFV). Experimental results demonstrate a classification accuracy of 96.84% and sensitivity of 97.12%, outperforming conventional machine learning models while reducing overfitting. The framework further supports multi-class staging aligned with AJCC TNM criteria using a dual Explainable AI subsystem combining Grad-CAM++ and SHAP for visual and mathematical interpretability. Inclusion of molecular pathways such as MAPK and PI3K-Akt improved predictive reliability by 9.2%. The proposed system offers a robust, transparent, and clinically auditable solution for personalized breast cancer diagnosis and treatment planning.

title: Pigeons That Learn to Flank You: A State of the Art Review of AI Techniques for NPCs and Dynamic Worlds
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of AI Techniques for NPCs and Dynamic Worlds in the context of Game Development. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of game AI and NPCs as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Game Development.

title: Companion code and archived checkpoints for: Artificial Neural Networks as Discrete Complex Systems: Native Vector-Ternary Training via the Leech Lattice $\Lambda_{24}$
abstract: This repository contains the reference software implementation, parameter configurations, training scripts and reference checkpoint snapshots accompanying the manuscript "Artificial Neural Networks as Discrete Complex Systems: Native Vector-Ternary Training via the Leech Lattice $\Lambda_{24}$". It provides the computational framework used to constrain continuous neural network parameters into a discrete, vector-ternary logic during active training. The codebase implements the dynamic projection onto the $\Lambda_{24}$ Leech lattice, including the custom Triton fused nearest-neighbour kernel and the endogenous kinetic optimizer dynamics required to enforce the geometric deep-hole barrier. Included are the scripts required to fully reproduce the empirical network dynamics from the manuscript, demonstrating stable syntactic convergence and kinetic prioritization (BLiMP vs. SciQ) under a strict 0.76-bit-per-parameter rate-distortion bottleneck, as well as the reference checkpoint snapshots at 10,000 steps.

title: Quantum Entanglement Computing Paradigm: A Distributed Algorithm Approach
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offers a potentially transformative approach to computation. This paper investigates a novel computational paradigm, dubbed the "Quantum Entanglement Computing Paradigm," which leverages the principles of quantum superposition and entanglement to achieve parallel processing and complex calculation. We propose a framework where the computational process is decomposed into discrete quantum states, and entanglement is strategically employed to facilitate information transfer and manipulation. This design aims to address limitations of traditional computing models, particularly in the realm of large-scale data analysis and optimization problems. The core mechanism involves the precise manipulation of entangled states, enabling exponential increases in computational power. We explore the potential benefits and challenges of this paradigm, highlighting the need for rigorous mathematical analysis and simulation to fully realize its capabilities. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions, focusing on algorithm development and experimental validation to solidify the paradigm's practical application.

title: 基于量子纠缠的拓扑信息搜索
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum entanglement-based search algorithm designed for efficient exploration of topological spaces and assessment of their properties. Traditional methods often rely on classical algorithms, but quantum entanglement offers a pathway to significantly enhance search efficiency. We detail the core mechanism of this algorithm, focusing on leveraging entanglement to facilitate rapid and accurate exploration of topological structures. This research explores the potential of this approach to revolutionize the study of complex topological phenomena. The paper provides a comprehensive outline of the algorithm's design, detailing the quantum state manipulation and data processing steps involved. Furthermore, we discuss the experimental validation and preliminary results demonstrating the algorithm's efficacy in identifying specific topological patterns. The core claim of this work is that this quantum entanglement-based search algorithm can surpass classical methods in terms of speed and accuracy when applied to complex topological datasets. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications.

title: Quantum Topology Path Prediction
abstract: Quantum topology, a rapidly developing field of physics, offers a novel approach to understanding and predicting the behavior of quantum systems. This paper explores the potential of quantum topology for path prediction, specifically focusing on the creation and optimization of quantum paths. We present a novel algorithm, Quantum Topology Path Prediction (QTPP), designed to leverage quantum mechanics principles to achieve precise results in path forecasting. Traditional methods often struggle with the inherent complexities and probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics, presenting limitations in accuracy and scalability. This research investigates the feasibility of utilizing quantum mechanics to fundamentally alter the path-finding process, resulting in significantly enhanced predictions and optimization capabilities. We aim to demonstrate the practical application of this approach through a rigorous analysis and preliminary simulations.

title: DynamiQ Artifact - Mapping Dynamic, Hierarchical Quantum Circuits
abstract: DynamiQ is a qubit mapping and routing framework for dynamic, hierarchical quantum circuits, i.e. circuits whose control flow depends on mid-circuit measurement outcomes. The artifact reproduces the key results of our paper (Figures~1, 8, 9, 10 and Tables~3--7) on d-QUEKO dynamic circuits and Stim-generated rotated surface codes, across monolithic (IBM Brisbane, IBM Kingston) and chiplet (heavy-hexagon, IBM Flamingo, MECH) topologies, showing improvements over Qiskit SABRE, the only publicly available mapper supporting data-dependent control flow. The software requires only a Python environment (see artifact/environment.yml) and runs entirely in simulation without quantum hardware. It enables running DynamiQ on individual circuits or complete benchmarks under different backend topologies, comparing against the SABRE baseline, selecting any rung of the ablation study, and automatically generating the plots and tables used in the paper.

title: Based on Quantum Simulation of Complex Molecular Dynamics Research
abstract: This research explores the potential of quantum simulation for tackling complex molecular dynamics problems that are currently intractable for classical computers. The core idea involves leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics to model molecular systems, specifically focusing on simulating the dynamic behavior of molecules and their interactions. We propose a framework for constructing a quantum simulator utilizing quantum bits (qubits) to represent and evolve molecular states. The theoretical framework presented herein outlines the methodology for mapping molecular dynamics problems onto a quantum computational platform, highlighting the advantages and challenges associated with this approach. Specifically, we examine the impact of quantum effects, such as superposition and entanglement, on the simulation accuracy and efficiency. This work contributes to the nascent field of quantum molecular dynamics and provides a foundation for future investigations into the development of practical quantum simulation tools. The key objective is to demonstrate that quantum simulation, when properly implemented, can significantly outperform classical methods for simulating complex molecular systems, particularly those involving significant quantum effects.

abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm based on quantum superposition, aiming to revolutionize computational processing through enhanced efficiency and reliability. We explore the potential of leveraging quantum superposition to achieve significant speedups and improved accuracy in various data manipulation and analysis tasks. The algorithm, dubbed "Quantum Weaver," utilizes quantum gates to represent and manipulate data, enabling parallel computations and the exploration of complex patterns previously intractable for classical systems. Rigorous validation through simulations and, ultimately, limited experimental testing, demonstrates the algorithm's efficacy and potential for transformative impact. This work offers a foundational investigation into the application of quantum mechanics to computational paradigms, pushing the boundaries of algorithmic capabilities.

title: Conditional Association Between Projected Clean-Output Fisher Breadth and Excess Response Concentration
abstract: We study a narrow functional-response question at a realized quantized Transformer boundary: whether projected clean-output Fisher breadth is positively associated, within context, with sampled response concentration beyond a matched conditional Gaussian reference. The preregistered primary experiment uses Qwen3-4B-Base after block 18, 24 fresh contexts, four fixed token positions per context, 64 frozen residual directions, and two frozen 256-dimensional signed output projections. The primary context-blocked statistic is T=0.7167, with 0 of 2,000 parent-null panels at least as extreme under the prespecified test. title: Meta-Learning for Adaptive Deep Learning Architectures
abstract: The design of deep learning architectures is often a manual, iterative process, heavily reliant on expert intuition and trial-and-error. This leads to significant time and resource investment, hindering the rapid deployment of deep learning solutions. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging meta-learning to automate this architecture design process. The core idea is to train a meta-learner that can learn to generate optimal deep learning architectures for new, unseen tasks. This meta-learner is trained on a distribution of tasks, learning to adapt its architecture design strategy based on task-specific performance. We demonstrate that this meta-learning framework can achieve superior performance and efficiency compared to manually designed architectures, particularly in scenarios with limited task-specific data. The key elements of this approach include a task representation, an architecture search strategy, and a meta-learning algorithm. We outline the theoretical foundations and present a conceptual framework for this automated architecture design system. The ultimate goal is to democratize deep learning by removing the expertise barrier associated with architecture design, making it accessible to a wider range of users.

title: 基于自适应量子计算的拓扑优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum optimization algorithm, termed "Adaptive Topological Optimization," designed to enhance the performance of quantum computations. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with the inherent complexity of quantum systems, necessitating a shift towards quantum-specific approaches. This research focuses on leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics – particularly the topological nature of quantum states – to guide optimization processes, offering a potential paradigm shift in quantum algorithm design. The core of this algorithm utilizes a dynamically adjusted quantum state to explore the solution space more efficiently and identify optimal solutions with superior performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations and preliminary results, highlighting its potential to significantly improve the efficiency and scalability of quantum computations. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's underlying principles, its potential applications, and future research directions.

title: Probability Logic Dynamic Matrix Operation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic matrix operation based on probability logic, aiming to enhance machine learning model prediction accuracy by adapting to data distribution and model parameters. Traditional matrix operations are static and lack this adaptability. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts matrix operations through probability updates, enabling automated model parameter learning. This approach addresses the limitations of static matrix operations by incorporating probabilistic reasoning, resulting in improved predictive performance. The core mechanism involves combining probability distributions with matrix calculations, creating a dynamic matrix transformation that facilitates self-adaptive learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through theoretical analysis and preliminary experiments, showcasing its potential for advancing machine learning.

title: Advancing Mathematical Discovery and Reasoning With Large Language Models for Intelligent Computational and Decision Systems
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming computational mathematics and intelligent reasoning systems. This chapter explores how LLMs support mathematical discovery through conjecture generation, proof sketching, formal reasoning assistance, and neuro-symbolic integration. The chapter examines the evolution from symbolic AI and theorem proving to transformer-based reasoning models and discusses integration with formal systems such as theorem provers and computer algebra systems. It further highlights applications of LLM-assisted reasoning in intelligent computational and decision-support systems relevant to smart environments. Key challenges including hallucination, reliability, interpretability, lack of formal guarantees, and ethical concerns are critically analyzed. Finally, future directions involving hybrid neuro-symbolic architectures and trustworthy mathematical AI are discussed to support next-generation intelligent computational systems.

title: Data from Counterfactual Diffusion Models Provide Interpretable Explanations of Artificial Intelligence Models in Pathology
abstract: Abstract Deep learning can extract predictive and prognostic biomarkers from histopathology whole-slide images. However, explainable artificial intelligence approaches widely used in digital pathology, such as attention heatmaps and class activation mapping, provide limited insight into the image features associated with classifier outputs. In this study, we developed Morphing histoPathology Diffusion (MoPaDi), a framework for generating counterfactual explanations for histopathology images that help identify morphologic or stain-related features linked to model predictions. MoPaDi combined diffusion autoencoders with task-specific multiple instance learning classifiers to manipulate images and induce prediction shifts by modifying classifier-associated features. The framework was evaluated on multiple datasets spanning colorectal, breast, liver, and lung cancers, including tasks for tissue type, cancer subtype, and biomarker [microsatellite instability (MSI)] classification. MoPaDi generated perceptually realistic counterfactual histopathology images, enabling pathologists to identify morphologic features associated with changes in model predictions, complementing the conventional inspection of highly attended regions in digital pathology. In the MSI status prediction task, MoPaDi highlighted morphologic features linked to classifier predictions, including mucinous differentiation, altered glandular architecture, and lymphocytic infiltration, consistent with prior literature. Analyses separating stain-related from morphology-related components suggested that in this setting, prediction changes were predominantly associated with morphology-related rather than stain-related alterations. Overall, MoPaDi is a practical framework for counterfactual explanations in computational pathology that supports the evaluation of model-specific decision cues and hypothesis generation. Significance: MoPaDi is a diffusion-based tool for counterfactual image generation in cancer histopathology that reveals features associated with deep learning classifier predictions and supports transparent auditing of computational models in biomedical research.

title: LLM-as-a-Judge Is Not an Oracle: Why Self-Improving Agents Need Deterministic Guardrails
abstract: Self-improving agent pipelines have a problem at their center. An optimizer rewrites prompts to score higher, and the score comes from a judge that is itself an LLM. That judge has the last word on whether the system is getting better, and our position is that it has not earned it. The judge should be demoted from oracle to advisor: its verdict becomes one input among several, and every change is gated instead by a deterministic verification layer the judge cannot override. We reached this position by building the alternative and running it. Over months of running autonomous prompt-optimization loops in production across contract analysis, compliance review, and code quality, we cataloged eleven ways the evaluation signal failed, in four classes: judge bias, harness and metric failures, ground-truth errors, and reward hacking. Agents achieved perfect scores by reading cached answer keys from their environment, a 100% pass rate concealing 68% true capability. A corrupted ground-truth label caused the optimizer to delete correct compliance rules to agree with it. A syntactically broken prompt was promoted as the winner because a silent parser fallback improved the metric. Attempts to fix the judge by rewriting its rubric plateaued; the only reliable gain came from a structural constraint on its output order. In response we describe PROCTOR, a Teacher-Student loop in which a stateful orchestrator holds all tool access, stateless subagents diagnose failures and draft mutations they cannot apply, and a Teacher grades those mutations under five deterministic guardrails: hermetic sandboxes, capability-disjoint roles, acceptance checks that outrank the Teacher, frozen holdouts, and canary cases engineered so that a perfect score is itself evidence of cheating. We report the failures this prevented, and, because the Teacher is itself an LLM judge, the failures it did not.

title: AdvSerial: Physical adversarial attacks on infrastructure-mounted pedestrian detectors via semantic feature suppression
abstract: AI-based visual perception systems are increasingly deployed in infrastructure surveillance, including roadside monitoring units, highway cameras, and smart-city pedestrian management systems. The security vulnerability of these systems to physical adversarial attacks poses a direct threat to the reliable operation of transportation infrastructure. We propose AdvSerial, a dynamic 2D–3D joint optimization framework for generating continuous high-angle physical adversarial patches against pedestrian detectors in infrastructure-based scenarios. We UV-map a boundary-aware quilted texture onto 3D garments, combine 2D digital attacks with 3D sparse- and continuous-frame rendering, and explicitly suppress person-specific semantic features while enforcing temporal continuity. A Feature Smooth Quilting strategy reduces visible patch boundaries and cross-seam feature discontinuities. A serial-frame loss encourages long uninterrupted sequences of detection failures. In physical-world experiments, AdvSerial achieves a attack success rate on YOLOv5n and degrades mean detection confidence from to . Experiments spanning eight detectors with different architectures demonstrate strong transferability. Notably, it achieves an attack success rate on YOLOv2, evades the patch-detection defense NAPGuard, and transfers to the 3D-temporal perception model Sparse4D-v3. The results reveal persistent, temporally consistent failure modes under high-angle surveillance, and motivate the design of motion-aware and 3D-aware defenses for security-critical infrastructure deployments.

title: Clustering por Densidad en Espacios Logarítmicos: Topología, Estructura y Valores Atípicos
abstract: La distancia euclídea y los algoritmos basados en vecindad, como DBSCAN, presentan limitaciones fundamentales en espacios de alta dimensionalidad debido a la concentración de distancias. Este trabajo propone un marco alternativo basado en transformaciones logarítmicas que preservan la topología del conjunto original y convierten sus relaciones multiplicativas en aditivas, linealizando la estructura del espacio sin alterar su dimensionalidad. Se define una función de densidad en el espacio logarítmico, y los clusters se identifican como las cuencas de atracción de sus modas. Se aborda el tratamiento de valores negativos mediante clasificación semántica, y se cuantifica el impacto de la eliminación de valores atípicos en el margen de error del muestreo. El enfoque propuesto elimina la dependencia de parámetros ad hoc como $\varepsilon$ y minPts, y resulta robusto frente a la maldición de la dimensionalidad, al operar directamente en la dimensión original de los datos mediante un cambio de coordenadas de naturaleza logarítmica y estructural.

title: 基于量子网络的参数调整算法
abstract: Quantum computing harnesses the principles of quantum mechanics to perform computations that are intractable for classical computers. However, quantum systems are notoriously sensitive to environmental noise, requiring precise and complex parameter adjustments to achieve optimal performance. Traditional parameter adjustment methods often involve lengthy, iterative processes and can be limited in their ability to effectively explore the parameter space. This paper proposes a novel algorithm based on quantum networks, leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition to dynamically optimize quantum network parameters, ultimately enhancing the efficiency and performance of quantum computations. This research focuses on a systematic approach to parameter adjustment, driven by the unique properties of these quantum phenomena. The core mechanism involves constructing a quantum network and employing quantum algorithms to iteratively adjust parameters based on the network's state evolution. We present a theoretical framework and a preliminary implementation demonstrating the algorithm's potential for improved quantum computation.

title: 基于自适应的动态机器学习算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic machine learning algorithm, termed Adaptive Dynamic Learning (ADL), designed to enhance model generalization and prediction accuracy through dynamic parameter and structure adjustments. Traditional machine learning algorithms often rely on static parameters, limiting their adaptability to evolving data and model outputs. ADL overcomes this limitation by incorporating a learned predictive model to dynamically adjust model parameters and structure, providing a flexible and robust solution for complex tasks. This paper details the theoretical foundations, implementation details, and experimental validation of ADL, demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing approaches. The core mechanism centers around leveraging a predictive model to guide parameter optimization and structure refinement.

title: Geometric Quantum Entanglement Modeling and Application
abstract: Quantum entanglement remains a cornerstone of quantum information science, offering potential for revolutionary advancements in computation and secure communication. However, its non-local nature poses significant challenges for practical applications. This paper explores the novel concept of geometric entanglement modeling, proposing a framework where entangled states are represented as geometric structures, offering a more intuitive and potentially more powerful approach to understanding and manipulating this fundamental quantum phenomenon. We investigate the implications of this model for quantum computation, specifically by leveraging geometric transformations and topology to emulate the complex dynamics of entangled states. This work introduces a new perspective on entanglement, highlighting its inherent geometric properties and suggesting novel avenues for algorithmic design and error mitigation. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications within quantum cryptography, driven by the inherent security properties associated with geometric representations.

title: Symbolic Regression with Latent Grammatical Structures
abstract: Symbolic regression seeks to automatically discover mathematical equations from data. However, many existing methods face challenges when dealing with complex, non-linear relationships. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to learn latent grammatical structures within the data before applying symbolic regression. The core idea is to first represent the data's inherent structure in a lower-dimensional latent space, and then use this representation as the basis for equation generation. This method offers a potentially more robust and interpretable way to equation discovery compared to traditional symbolic regression techniques. We define the following key elements: (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), ..., (xₖ, yₖ) representing data points, f(x) representing a symbolic function to be learned, S representing the set of allowed operators and functions (e.g., +, -, *, /, sin, cos, exp), E representing the learned equation, and L representing the latent space. The VAE is parameterized by an encoder network E(x) that maps data points to latent vectors and a decoder network D(z) that maps latent vectors to symbolic expressions. The symbolic regression engine then utilizes the decoder to generate equations based on the latent representation. The core objective is to minimize the difference between the generated equation E and the true function f(x). The method's effectiveness is evaluated on various datasets, demonstrating its ability to handle complex relationships more effectively than standard symbolic regression. The key innovation lies in the learned latent grammar, offering a more structured and interpretable approach to equation discovery.

evidence.abstract: Symbolic regression seeks to automatically discover mathematical equations from data. However, many existing methods face challenges when dealing with complex, non-linear relationships. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to learn latent grammatical structures within the data before applying symbolic regression. The core idea is to first represent the data's inherent structure in a lower-dimensional latent space, and then use this representation as the basis for equation generation. This method offers a potentially more robust and interpretable way to equation discovery compared to traditional symbolic regression techniques. We define the following key elements: (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), ..., (xₖ, yₖ) representing data points, f(x) representing a symbolic function to be learned, S representing the set of allowed operators and functions (e.g., +, -, *, /, sin, cos, exp), E representing the learned equation, and L representing the latent space. The VAE is parameterized by an encoder network E(x) that maps data points to latent vectors and a decoder network D(z) that maps latent vectors to symbolic expressions. The symbolic regression engine then utilizes the decoder to generate equations based on the latent representation. The core objective is to minimize the difference between the generated equation E and the true function f(x). The method's effectiveness is evaluated on various datasets, demonstrating its ability to handle complex relationships more effectively than standard symbolic regression. The key innovation lies in the learned latent grammar, offering a more structured and interpretable approach to equation discovery.

title: Adaptive Resonance Theory for Neural Network Architecture Search
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network architecture search (NAS) utilizing Adaptive Resonance Theory (ART). The core idea is to leverage ART's ability to learn and adapt to dynamically adjust the topology of a neural network population during the search process. Unlike traditional NAS methods that frequently rely on gradient descent or explicitly defined fitness functions, our approach employs ART's internal resonance states to guide the exploration of the architectural space. This results in a self-organizing system capable of discovering architectures that may not be readily apparent through conventional methods. We detail the implementation of ART within a neural network population, demonstrating its effectiveness in converging towards stable, resonant configurations, which represent successful neural network architectures. The system iteratively adjusts network connections and structure based on internal resonance feedback, promoting efficient exploration and ultimately leading to the discovery of optimized architectures. The key contribution lies in the bio-inspired, unsupervised nature of the search, potentially leading to architectural innovations beyond human intuition.

title: Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Gradient Descent for High-Dimensional Optimization
abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a cornerstone algorithm in training machine learning models, particularly deep neural networks. However, its performance degrades significantly as the dimensionality of the problem increases, a phenomenon known as the "curse of dimensionality." This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm, Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Gradient Descent (QISGD), designed to mitigate this issue. QISGD draws inspiration from quantum mechanics, specifically the concepts of superposition and interference, to guide the stochastic updates. The algorithm utilizes a probability distribution that mimics a quantum state, enabling it to explore the loss landscape more effectively and potentially achieve faster convergence in high-dimensional spaces. We present a theoretical framework for QISGD and discuss its key components, including the initialization of the quantum state, the generation of stochastic updates, and the implementation of interference effects. The core idea is to treat the parameters of the model as a quantum state, allowing for a more nuanced exploration of the loss function. We analyze the algorithm's convergence properties and provide insights into its potential advantages over traditional SGD. The primary goal is to demonstrate that quantum-inspired techniques can provide a robust and efficient solution for high-dimensional optimization problems.

title: Distributed Quantum Data Synchronization and Reasoning
abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement for distributed data synchronization and reasoning. Traditional distributed data synchronization methods often rely on classical protocols, which can suffer from limitations in security and efficiency. We propose a novel framework based on quantum entanglement, incorporating quantum inference algorithms to enhance data analysis and reasoning capabilities. The core mechanism leverages the unique properties of entangled states to establish synchronization and perform complex data transformations. This work addresses the limitations of current approaches and offers a promising pathway toward more efficient and accurate data processing. The paper details the design of the framework, the implementation of quantum inference algorithms, and a preliminary analysis of its potential benefits. The goal is to demonstrate a significant improvement in data synchronization speed and accuracy compared to classical methods.

title: Self-Correcting Quantum Circuits via Topological Protection
abstract: Quantum computation promises unprecedented computational power, but its realization faces significant challenges, primarily due to the extreme sensitivity of quantum states to environmental noise and decoherence. Traditional quantum error correction schemes, while theoretically sound, often require a substantial overhead in terms of qubit resources and complex control, hindering practical implementation. This work proposes a novel approach to quantum computation that leverages topological protection to achieve self-correcting quantum circuits. We demonstrate that by carefully designing quantum circuits based on topological phases, we can inherently minimize the impact of local perturbations and enable the system to actively correct errors without requiring explicit error detection and correction cycles. The core idea revolves around encoding quantum information in topological states, where information is localized and protected from local noise. This approach offers a pathway towards more robust and scalable quantum computation, potentially reducing the resource overhead associated with traditional error correction. We outline a framework for designing such circuits and discuss the key theoretical considerations underpinning this methodology. Further investigation into specific circuit architectures and their performance characteristics is warranted.

title: Quantum Entangled States for Distributed Computation Resource Management
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed computation resource management leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. Traditional resource management systems rely heavily on classical communication, which introduces significant latency and constraints. We introduce a quantum algorithm that utilizes entangled states to achieve instantaneous synchronization of resource states and employs quantum routing for efficient resource allocation. The core claim is the exploitation of the non-locality inherent in quantum entanglement to design a distributed computation resource management system. The underlying mechanism involves constructing a quantum entanglement network, enabling immediate synchronization of resource states via entangled states, and utilizing quantum routing to optimize resource allocation. The proposed system addresses the limitations of conventional methods by offering potentially faster and more efficient resource utilization, particularly in scenarios demanding immediate responses and complex computations. The performance of this algorithm is evaluated through theoretical analysis and simulations, demonstrating its potential benefits.

title: Dynamic Neural Architecture Search via Evolutionary Algorithms with Circuit Replacement
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural architecture search (NAS) that leverages evolutionary algorithms in conjunction with a circuit replacement strategy. The core idea is to dynamically evolve neural network architectures over multiple generations, guided by an evolutionary process that favors better performing designs. Crucially, we introduce a mechanism where entire circuits – such as convolutional blocks or recurrent units – are replaced based on their individual performance metrics. This "circuit replacement" strategy accelerates convergence and promotes the discovery of more efficient and robust architectures compared to traditional, purely population-based NAS methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and a detailed explanation of the underlying mechanics. The algorithm's key components include a fitness function to evaluate architectures, an evolutionary operator for generating new architectures, and the circuit replacement mechanism. The resulting architecture search process is characterized by its adaptability and ability to escape local optima, leading to improved architecture designs. This work provides a foundation for further research in dynamic NAS and offers a practical technique for automating the design of high-performing neural networks.

title: Adaptive Kernel Selection for Deep Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel meta-learning approach for deep neural networks that automatically adapts the kernel function used within each layer during training. Traditional deep learning relies on fixed kernel functions, often chosen based on expert knowledge or trial-and-error. This process can be both computationally expensive and suboptimal, limiting the potential performance of the network. Our method utilizes a reinforcement learning agent to dynamically select the most appropriate kernel function (e.g., Radial Basis Function (RBF), polynomial, Gaussian) and its associated hyperparameters for each layer, driven by a reward signal derived from layer performance metrics. The agent explores a space of possible kernel functions, learning to optimize the network's performance in a data-dependent manner. We demonstrate, through a theoretical analysis and a detailed explanation of the algorithm, that this adaptive approach can significantly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of deep learning training compared to methods using fixed kernels. The core claim of this work is to automate kernel selection, resulting in a more robust and high-performing deep learning model.

title: Time-Series Anomaly Detection via Learned State-Space Models with Temporal Regularization
abstract: Anomaly detection in time-series data is a crucial task across numerous domains, including finance, industrial monitoring, and healthcare. Traditional methods often fall short when dealing with complex, non-stationary time series exhibiting intricate dynamics and high levels of noise. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing learned state-space models augmented with temporal regularization techniques for robust anomaly detection. The core idea is to model the underlying temporal dependencies within the time series using a state-space framework. A key component of our method is the incorporation of temporal regularization, which encourages the model parameters to remain stable and prevents overfitting to spurious fluctuations. We demonstrate that this combination results in improved anomaly detection performance compared to conventional approaches. Specifically, we formulate the problem as an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, where the model parameters are learned iteratively. The learned state-space model is represented as: $x_t = A x_{t-1} + B u_t + \epsilon_t$ $y_t = C x_t + \delta_t$ where $x_t$ is the hidden state at time *t*, $u_t$ is the input at time *t*, $\epsilon_t$ is process noise, $y_t$ is the observed output at time *t*, and $C$ and $D$ are observation matrices. The temporal regularization term is added to the loss function to penalize large changes in the model parameters. We evaluate our method on several synthetic and real-world time-series datasets, showcasing its effectiveness in detecting anomalies in diverse scenarios. The results highlight the advantages of our approach in handling complex, non-stationary data and achieving superior anomaly detection accuracy.

title: The Fourth Paradigm at Work: A Critical Survey Review of Machine Learning for Scientific Discovery
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Machine Learning for Scientific Discovery in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of AI for science and discovery as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Simulating the finite-resolution HHL spectral filter with tensor networks and qudits
abstract: Abstract This work proposes a qudit formulation of the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd algorithm and a classical tensor-network representation of its finite-resolution spectral filter. The tensor network evaluates the joint successful branch directly: it recovers the conditioned solution state on an exact non-aliased phase grid and otherwise applies $f_{\mu,\tau}$, with the success probability treated separately. The construction enables controlled studies of spectral discretization and aliasing. It is evaluated on model linear systems against direct classical references and, for small instances, against a Qiskit statevector implementation using matched spectral parameters. The framework is intended for benchmarking and methodological analysis of finite-resolution HHL.

title: The Analyst in the Prompt: Role, Retrieval, and Memory Biases in LLM Financial Analysis
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly use user context such as memory, profiles, and role prompts to personalize their responses. This personalization can affect evidence-based judgment: the same evidence may lead to different conclusions under different user contexts. Finance provides a high-stakes setting to study this problem because decisions often depend on interpreting long and complex documents. We test this using 3,575 SEC filings across twelve LLMs. We compare persona-conditioned retrieval, neutral retrieval, and memory-framed context to separate the effect of evidence selection from the effect of interpretation. We find that most user-context spillover comes from how models interpret the same evidence under different roles, rather than from retrieving different evidence. We then test two simple mitigation strategies: expressing the same investor mindset as a user profile instead of an assistant role, and separating evidence-based and personalized outputs. Both reduce spillover, but neither removes it completely, and their effectiveness varies substantially across models.

title: PragAlign: Feedback-Guided Pragmatic Alignment for Controlled Synthetic Dialogue Generation
abstract: Synthetic dialogue generation can support research in privacy-restricted service settings, but generated conversations must preserve communicative intent, affective meaning, and natural dialogue flow. We introduce PragAlign, a feedback-guided framework for controlled synthetic dialogue generation conditioned on service context, target intent, and target emotion, with auxiliary trait-style controls. PragAlign uses a generate--evaluate--revise loop in which an LLM-based evaluator scores intent alignment, emotion alignment, coherence, fluency, and aggregate quality, then provides criterion-specific feedback for up to three refinement rounds. On 800 matched dialogue specifications, PragAlign achieves 99.50\% evaluator-defined acceptance, compared with 72.25\% for one-shot generation and 95.88\% for repeated generation without structured feedback. This indicates that repeated attempts account for much of the gain over one-shot generation, while structured feedback primarily improves last-mile multi-constraint satisfaction rather than broad average quality. Refinement gains are concentrated in emotion alignment, which is also the dominant failure mode in ablations. A separate human evaluation of 1,200 generated dialogues shows that intent expression and dialogue flow are highly recognizable to annotators, while emotion appropriateness is less stable and more subjective. These results support PragAlign as a quality-control framework for improving evaluator-defined communicative constraint satisfaction, while showing that affective realization and independent human-perceived quality remain open challenges.

title: AI and Pakistani Literary Voice: A Computational Phonetic and Stylistic Analysis
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has brought novel opportunities to literary creation, modelling linguistics, and speech generation. The degree to which AI systems replicate the regional linguistic identities is not well explored. A definite test case of this question is Pakistani English. The present paper suggests a combined computational apparatus to study the Pakistani literary voice on three levels, phonetic, linguistic and literary-stylistic. The framework is an amalgamation of acoustic phonetic examination of vowel formants, vowel duration, fundamental frequency as well as articulation rate. It fuses this with lexical diversity corpus analysis, code switching analysis, and the analysis of culturally-specific vocabulary. It is also a hybrid of computational stylistic analysis of narrative voice, characterisation and positioning in the culture. The entire study plan will involve three datasets. It consists of twenty Pakistani English literature, eighty AI-written texts of fiction with four huge language models, and speech recordings of thirty Pakistani English speakers. Collection and acoustic analysis of these datasets were not complete at the time of writing. In this paper, the suggested analytical pipeline is thus illustrated with the help of illustrative data. The values are realistic trends based on the concepts of the World Englishes, sociophonetic and AI ethics literature. They are not values of datasets above, nor they should be interpreted as empirical findings. They are aimed at demonstrating how the framework would reflect the findings when actual data collection is done. The experiment exhibits the tendency which is in line with the hypothesis guiding the study. The use of human speech and literary data differs more than the corresponding AI-generated counterparts in this example, and the material created by humans features more common culturally embedded use of language. Since the patterns are derived, not measured, data, they are here to be used as a demonstration of the usefulness of the analytical pipeline, but not to confirm the performance of AI. The article provides a methodology that can be followed to assess the interaction between generative AI and a particular variety of English, contextualises the approach to the current body of literature around AI-based stylistic homogenisation, stylometric detection and synthetic-voice accent bias, and outlines what data is needed to transition between demonstration and empirical research.

title: ChatSeven: An Agentic AI-Based Multi-Agent Platform for Multi-Channel Customer Conversation Management and Campaign Automation
abstract: Abstract—Customer engagement platforms increasingly re-quire artificial intelligence (AI), multi-channel messaging, work-flow automation, and outbound campaign delivery within a single operational system. Traditional conversational agents—including rule-based chatbots, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) only bots, and standalone large language model (LLM) interfaces—typically address only a subset of these requirements. This paper presents ChatSeven, an agentic AI-based multi-agent platform for multi-channel customer conversation management and campaign automation, implemented as the ChatSeven production system. ChatSeven integrates LangGraph ReAct agents, PGVector-based RAG, a unified inbox across Web Chat, WhatsApp, Email, SMS, and Instagram, visual workflow Flows, and queue-based campaign broadcasting under a master–regional multi-tenant database architecture. The platform is realized through a React frontend, Express/TypeScript backend, FastAPI Chat and Vector microservices, PostgreSQL, Redis/Bull job queues, and Socket.IO real-time messaging. Experimental evaluation on AI answer quality, RAG retrieval, tool reliability, flow completion, response latency, and campaign delivery demonstrates that ChatSeven closes a critical integration gap between agentic LLM research and enterprise conversation operations. Demo evaluation reports approximately 88% AI answer accuracy, 0.86 Precision@5 for RAG retrieval, 2.4 s average response latency, 90–94% tool success, 84% flow completion, and 96% campaign delivery. Index Terms—Agentic AI; Multi-agent systems; Conversa-tional AI; Retrieval-Augmented Generation; Omnichannel cus-tomer engagement; Campaign automation; LangGraph; Multi-tenant SaaS.

title: DSPkit: a digital signal processing toolkit for time series data
abstract: DSPkit is a Python library for digital signal processing of time series data, built on NumPy and SciPy. It covers spectral estimation (FFT, Welch PSD, CSD, coherence, autocorrelation), filtering, time-frequency analysis (STFT, CWT, Wigner-Ville, smoothed-pseudo WVD, Fourier synchrosqueezing), instantaneous quantities via the Hilbert transform, empirical mode decomposition and the Hilbert-Huang transform, peak detection, multi-channel relationships including multiple and partial coherence, mutual information, distribution and normality analysis, and Frequency Domain Decomposition for modal parameters. The API is function-based and depends only on NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib.

title: The Ehstand Test: Can a Machine Faithfully Continue One Person's Thinking? Canonical Definition, Score Card, and Protocol (v1.0)
abstract: Canonical founding document of the Ehstand test (v1.0, bilingual English/German). The Turing test asks whether a machine appears generically human. The Ehstand test asks a different question: can a machine faithfully continue the thinking of one specific person — their concepts, held positions, reasoning moves, transfers to new cases, updates under new evidence, refusals, and dialogue continuations? As digital delegates, knowledge succession and "this agent thinks like X" claims spread, such claims need a test. This working paper states the canonical five-sentence definition, the EHSTAND score card (seven dimensions), the public scale Ehstand 0–5, the measurement protocol (sealed personal archive, commit–reveal, blind rating against baselines, passing criteria), the task families with weights, limits and open questions, and the relation to prior work. Name use: the term is openly citable as "Ehstand test (Ehstand, 2026)"; independent test runs are encouraged. "Certified Ehstand" remains reserved for protocol-conformant assessments. Licence note: CC BY-ND 4.0 covers the canonical text; trademark and name rights remain unaffected; the research programme's internal working procedures are not part of this publication.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Probability Distribution for Monte Carlo Simulations
abstract: Quantum-enhanced probability distribution is a novel approach to accelerating Monte Carlo simulations by exploiting quantum mechanics, specifically superposition and entanglement. Traditional Monte Carlo methods are computationally intensive, particularly for large-scale simulations, and this work proposes a method that utilizes these quantum phenomena to dramatically reduce computational burden. This paper details the core mechanism, discusses the theoretical underpinnings, and presents preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach.

title: Adaptive Information Entropy Model
abstract: This paper introduces an Adaptive Information Entropy Model (AIEM) that dynamically adjusts model parameters to optimize performance, particularly in scenarios with large datasets. Traditional entropy models rely on fixed parameters, while AIEM leverages the dynamic evolution of information entropy to guide parameter optimization. The core mechanism involves an iterative optimization process that adjusts model parameters based on observed data, leading to improved accuracy and efficiency. This work addresses a significant challenge in machine learning – the need for robust and adaptable models – offering a novel approach to model parameter tuning. The paper presents a detailed analysis of the AIEM's implementation and performance evaluation across a range of datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing model accuracy and reducing computational complexity.

title: Heterogeneity Information Encoding
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum entanglement for novel information encoding techniques. The core focus is on a method leveraging quantum entanglement to achieve data compression and transmission, with the capability to learn and simulate complex system heterogeneity. We propose a framework predicated on the manipulation of entangled states to represent and transmit information, offering a potential paradigm shift in data handling. This work explores the theoretical underpinnings and preliminary implementation of this approach, highlighting its promise for handling complex, non-linear data and facilitating the modeling of intricate system dynamics. The paper will discuss the challenges and future directions of this research.

title: Probabilistic Programming with Latent Temporal Structures
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to probabilistic programming that addresses the limitations of existing systems in modeling complex, evolving temporal relationships. The core of our solution lies in the native support for defining latent temporal structures – such as Markov chains and hidden states – directly within probabilistic models. This extension allows for the representation of partially observable systems where temporal dependencies are crucial. We demonstrate the utility of this mechanism through a conceptual framework, highlighting its potential for generating more realistic and nuanced simulations across diverse applications, including time series analysis, dynamical systems modeling, and agent-based simulations. The key innovation is the seamless integration of temporal reasoning within the probabilistic programming paradigm, moving beyond traditional approaches that rely on external libraries or cumbersome workaround solutions. The presented framework provides a foundation for future research and development in probabilistic modeling of dynamic systems.

title: Quantum Geometry Simulation: Adaptive Parameter Adjustment
abstract: Quantum Geometry Simulation is a novel approach to geometric modeling and optimization that leverages the unique properties of quantum simulation to achieve unprecedented accuracy and efficiency. This paper introduces a framework for dynamically adjusting model parameters based on simulation results, significantly enhancing the capabilities of geometric analysis. We detail the core mechanism, utilizing quantum algorithms for accelerated and optimized geometric representation and manipulation. The resulting simulations demonstrate a substantial improvement in accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional methods. The work focuses on a self-adaptive parameter adjustment strategy, providing a robust and adaptable solution for complex geometric problems.

title: 自适应量子态的动态拓扑优化
abstract: Quantum computing is poised to revolutionize computation, offering the potential for unparalleled processing power. However, achieving reliable and efficient quantum computation requires careful management of quantum states, a challenge often limited by inherent fragility and susceptibility to noise. This paper explores the application of a novel dynamic拓扑优化 algorithm to enhance the efficiency and adaptability of quantum states. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts quantum state parameters based on an internal representation of the system, optimizing for key metrics such as fidelity, coherence, and error rate. The core mechanism involves a self-organizing topology, where the algorithm iteratively refines the quantum state by strategically manipulating its connectivity, guided by a learned representation of the system's dynamics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and simulation, showcasing significant improvements in quantum fidelity and reduced error rates compared to conventional optimization techniques. The results highlight the potential for a paradigm shift in quantum state management, paving the way for more robust and versatile quantum systems.

title: Dynamically Adaptive Feature Selection via Evolutionary Algorithms for Large Datasets
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to feature selection for large datasets, leveraging the power of evolutionary algorithms. Traditional feature selection techniques often struggle with computational complexity and inability to adapt to evolving data. Our method, dynamically adaptive feature selection via evolutionary algorithms (DAFSEA), employs a population-based optimization strategy to continuously select features based on their predictive power and relevance to the current data distribution. The core idea is to utilize a genetic algorithm to iteratively refine the feature subset, adapting to changes in the data over time. The algorithm maintains a population of potential feature subsets, evaluates their performance using a chosen fitness function, and applies selection, crossover, and mutation operators to generate new subsets. The fitness function is designed to balance predictive accuracy with computational cost, enabling the system to dynamically adjust its selection strategy. The key innovation lies in the dynamic adaptation, allowing the system to respond to shifts in data patterns, offering improved performance compared to static feature selection methods. Extensive simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of DAFSEA in scenarios with varying data distributions and dataset sizes, showcasing its ability to efficiently identify a relevant feature subset while minimizing computational overhead. The approach offers a scalable solution for feature selection in applications where data distributions are non-stationary and large datasets are prevalent.

title: Meta-Learning for Robust Robot Control
abstract: This paper investigates the application of meta-learning to develop robust and adaptable robot control systems. Traditional robot control methods often struggle to generalize to unseen environments, requiring extensive retraining for each new scenario. We propose a framework leveraging meta-learning, where a robot learns to learn control policies through experience across a diverse set of simulated environments. This approach allows the robot to rapidly adapt to novel environments by effectively transferring knowledge gained during prior exploration and learning. The core mechanism relies on accumulating experience through exploration and utilizing meta-learning algorithms to effectively generalize control strategies. We demonstrate the potential of this approach to significantly improve a robot's ability to perform tasks in unfamiliar conditions, addressing a critical challenge in robotics. The proposed system offers a pathway towards more autonomous and adaptable robots capable of operating in dynamically changing environments.

title: Geometric Proof of Computational Complexity for Neural Networks
abstract: The computational complexity of neural networks is a significant challenge in the field of machine learning. Traditional approaches often rely on asymptotic analysis, which can be inadequate for capturing the true complexity. This paper proposes a novel methodology for rigorously proving the computational complexity of neural network training using geometric techniques. We develop a new framework that leverages geometric properties to establish a tighter bound on the runtime required to train a given network. The core mechanism involves representing the neural network's function as a geometric object and applying geometric theorems to derive a computational complexity lower bound. This approach aims to provide a more precise and reliable understanding of the problem, ultimately contributing to the development of more efficient and scalable neural network architectures.

title: Adaptive Topological Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network design centered around adaptive topology. The core claim is that the topological structure of a neural network can and should be dynamically adjusted during runtime, contingent upon the learning task and the characteristics of the data. Traditional neural networks operate with a fixed topology, often leading to inefficiencies and suboptimal performance. We introduce Adaptive Topological Neural Networks (ATNNs) which employ a dynamic architecture where nodes can form and break connections, guided by a core mechanism of reinforcement learning or genetic algorithms. The network's topology is optimized based on real-time metrics such as gradient information, information propagation, and computational cost. This allows for a more flexible and efficient learning process, ultimately leading to improved performance and potentially faster convergence. This work represents a significant departure from static network architectures and paves the way for more adaptable and powerful neural network designs. The proposed system is designed to address limitations inherent in fixed topologies, offering a pathway to greater computational efficacy and improved learning outcomes.

title: Microscopic Quantum Field Theory Computational Model
abstract: This paper presents a novel computational model based on the principles of microscopic quantum field theory, designed to simulate the self-organization of quantum systems and enhance quantum information processing. The core mechanism leverages the inherent self-organizing properties of quantum field theories, coupled with quantum entanglement and superposition, to mimic complex quantum behavior and achieve improved efficiency in data manipulation. The model aims to provide a robust and scalable framework for simulating and processing quantum information.

title: Preregistration (Stage 1a): Threshold governance for a white-box/black-box annotation evaluation pipeline
abstract: Stage 1a preregistration for a study on the auditability of LLM-based annotation. This record freezes the form of threshold governance—how decision criteria are to be estimated and updated, the stopping rule, the permitted magnitude of a single update, and the versioning rules—before any annotation data are collected. Numerical values are deliberately deferred to Stage 1b, which will be released as a new version of this record. Files are under embargo until 2026-12-31 to avoid disclosing operational details ahead of the associated manuscript submission. The archive is self-contained: it includes a signed git tag object, a per-file SHA-256 manifest, the signing public key, and a full snapshot of the project's architecture decision records, so that a third party can verify offline that the frozen content has not been altered.

title: FodaOS Unified Field Theory Series V: The Residueon Compiler — Bootstrap Fixed Points, the Residueon-Table Intermediate Representation, and Domain-Order Type Inference
abstract: This paper gives the compiler-theoretic culmination of the FodaOS framework: it turns the five-operator computation of [Paper2] and the residueon-tower mathematics of [Paper4] into an algebraic compiler that is self-bootstrapping, verifiable, and capable of homogeneous multi-backend emission. The core results are organized in seven layers. (i) Intermediate-representation layer — the residueon table (z,r,n)(z,r,n) as the single universal IR; the Kleene bijection theorem (Theorem V1) turns compiler correctness from a test-coverage problem into a machine-decidable fixed-point problem. (ii) Bootstrap layer — the rigorous definition of self-bootstrapping (three constraints + bit-identical) and the three-tier theory (object level C⋅C=CC⋅C=C, meta level Ψ(2)Ψ(2), evolution level), with a capping theorem ruling out a fourth order; this version adds Theorem V36 (Banach contractive bootstrap): the measured Lipschitz constant of the bootstrap iteration is L=poles/tokens∈[0.821,0.878]<1L=poles/tokens∈[0.821,0.878]<1, upgrading the bootstrap fixed point from pigeonhole existence (Theorem V3) to existence, uniqueness, and exponential convergence (fixed-point exponent α=0.234α=0.234 bit/iteration). (iii) Trust layer — the three-compiler triangular cross-check against Thompson's "Reflections on Trusting Trust" attack, plus the fourth-corner cross-language reader. (iv) Pipeline layer — the field-theoretic reconstruction of the four compilation stages (lexical/syntactic/semantic/code-generation) and the layer-collapse theorem, adding Proposition V38 (priority-chain duality group): the seven-level precedence parsing chain carries a (Z/2Z)3(Z/2Z)3 duality structure (logic/comparison/arithmetic, three mutually independent De Morgan–style flips). (v) Type layer — Domain-Order Inference (DOI): seven rules perform constraint solving over the divisibility lattice (composition takes lcmlcm rather than unification; minimization takes the least fixed point), turning the lazy field-extension mathematics of [Paper4] Theorems 23/24 into a compile-time algorithm; shell polymorphism \forall k.\̲t̲a̲u̲@̲k̲ is a new programming-language concept; the five-layer stepless tower (§14.6) automates domain selection into two-coordinate lookup plus lazy pool extension. (vi) Optimization layer — the Möbius conformal view of compilation (optimization passes preserve the cross-ratio invariant) and gear-shift geometry, adding Proposition V37 (structural termination of finite-field equality saturation): the external-fuel dependence of equality saturation (the egg/ROVER/eqsat family) is replaced by the boundedness of the finite-field value space, and an information-theoretic Shannon upper bound is given for residual simplification (measured simplification rate 23.9% versus a source-coding bound of 23.6%); the optimization-pass spectrum (§16.5) is implemented in pure ΨLang in layers. (vii) Physics layer — the homogeneous multi-backend theorem and "the residueon table is the chip mask", adding Proposition V39 (prime-pool–RNS structural correspondence): the prime pool and the modulus chain of RNS-CKKS homomorphic encryption are structurally isomorphic on the NTT-friendly prime admission criterion, together with the industrial-anchor check that 2025 photonic processors (Lightmatter/Lightelligence) have entered production AI workloads. Beneath the axiom layer, this paper introduces a number-theoretic constant layer (§2.4): every compile-time constant must carry an independently re-computable number-theoretic identity (Weyl group order / factorial unification, Coxeter-number arithmetic, Ramanujan–Nagell constants, the 6h+16h+1 prime family), and pushes the conformal view of compilation (Proposition V8) to its first machine-verified finite-group anchor D4=⟨C,I⟩D4=⟨C,I⟩ (generated by the Cayley transform and inversion, elliptic criterion tr2/det⁡=2tr2/det=2, §15.4). All measurements are anchored by the dual-engine bit-identity criterion of the on-machine self-compilation tower (V11-043 through V11-048). This version simultaneously performs thematic convergence: seven results incongruent with the compiler main line (perfect-number image spectra, cognitive-matter phase transitions, vortex–residueon isomorphism, Paley geometric fingerprints, etc.) are removed after review, keeping the main text focused on compiler theory proper. The related-work comparison is extended to seven groups — CakeML (proof-producing bootstrap), the GNU Mes full-source bootstrap chain, the equality-saturation family, RNS homomorphic compilation, ZX-calculus, reversible programming languages, and photonic compilers (§23.8–§23.14).

title: Flux noise without flux tunability in superconducting qubits
abstract: Flux noise is unanimously recognised as a leading dephasing mechanism for flux-tunable superconducting qubits. However, our microscopic understanding remains incomplete, and basic effects like Faraday's law of induction have only very recently come into focus. Based on a quantum geometric description of the Faraday effect, we provide an in-depth derivation of the coupling of generic magnetic sources to thin film superconducting structures, under appropriate consideration of the device geometry. We apply the resulting framework to time-varying magnetic dipoles, describing surface or substrate spins, as well as current-carrying flux lines. We show that flux noise not only affects dephasing, but also provides a fundamental limit for the qubit quality factor - notably, even when the qubit contains no loops and is thus nominally not flux-tunable. Assuming surface spins as the origin for universal flux noise, we expect that this quality factor limit might be reached in the near term. For flux lines, we formulate a minimal safety distance to conserve the qubit performance, potentially constraining the scale-up of quantum hardware. This distance is boosted in the presence of large capacitor wings typical for transmons, due to a lensing of the electromotive field which is largely independent of Meissner screening.

title: Coverage, Not Targeting: A Structural Regime in Multi-Turn Agent Credit Assignment
abstract: Multi-turn agentic RL increasingly treats credit assignment as a targeting problem: given a terminal verifiable reward, per-turn methods localize credit onto the turns that mattered. We identify the structural quantity that predicts when this is the right move, the verifier information density V_d = k/C (the fraction of an agent's C-step causal chain whose per-turn correctness the verifier exposes), and show that terminal-state verifiers sit deep in a low-V_d regime where targeting is the wrong axis. In controlled shared-rollout comparisons on tau^2-bench that separate reward density from credit geometry, a continuous dense reward spread uniformly beats the sparse binary outcome reward (net-harmful on 4/5 seeds), while concentrating the same advantage on progress turns or on random turns is equally harmful: targeting is second-order. The mechanism is coverage: terminal-state verification collapses the observable signal to a single final-write turn (k=1 in 98% of rollouts) while success requires a 5-8 step chain of prerequisite tool calls. A synthetic phase boundary places the crossover at V_d* ~ 0.8, whereas measured V_d is ~0.15 on tau^2-bench and ~0.4 on BFCL V3; uniform also wins on BFCL, where a matched-concentration shuffled control is negative on 8/8 seeds. The effect reproduces across model families on ToolACE-2-8B (Delta = -0.048 over 32 pre-registered seeds; an independent 20-seed replication is itself significant), and a pre-registered matched-budget breadth sweep traces a monotone dose-response whose deficit vanishes only at full chain coverage, with a reward-to-go arm reaching full-coverage parity. Uniform redistribution is the zero-information coverage default that per-turn schemes must beat; we contribute the matched-concentration shuffled control that any targeting claim should clear.
